findings.title: WordPress core is running an outdated, unsupported version (5.2)
findings.explanation: The site is running WordPress 5.2, which was released years ago and no longer receives security updates. Outdated WordPress installs are one of the most common ways attackers break into small business websites, since known vulnerabilities are public and easily automated against.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade WordPress core to the latest stable release as soon as possible, taking a backup first.

findings.title: Server is running an old, end-of-life PHP version (7.2.1)
findings.explanation: The X-Powered-By header shows PHP 7.2.1, a version that has been end-of-life for years and no longer receives security patches. Combined with the outdated WordPress install, this significantly increases the risk of the site being compromised.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade the server's PHP version to a currently supported release (PHP 8.1 or newer) after testing plugin/theme compatibility.

findings.title: WordPress REST API exposes user account information
findings.explanation: The WordPress REST API is publicly revealing 3 user accounts. Attackers commonly use this to discover valid usernames, then target those accounts with password-guessing attacks.
findings.recommendation: Restrict or disable the REST API user endpoint (e.g. via a security plugin) so usernames aren't publicly listable.

findings.title: XML-RPC endpoint is enabled
findings.explanation: XML-RPC is turned on, which is frequently abused for brute-force login attempts and to amplify denial-of-service attacks against the site.
findings.recommendation: Disable XML-RPC unless it's specifically required by a plugin or service, either via a security plugin or server-level rule.

findings.title: WordPress readme.html file is publicly accessible
findings.explanation: The default readme.html file is reachable, which can confirm the exact WordPress version to visitors and potential attackers, making it easier for them to look up matching known vulnerabilities.
findings.recommendation: Remove or block access to readme.html on the server.

findings.title: No DMARC record configured for the domain
findings.explanation: The domain has an SPF record but no DMARC record. Without DMARC, it's easier for scammers to send phishing emails that impersonate your domain, and you won't get reports of such abuse.
findings.recommendation: Add a DMARC TXT record (starting with a monitoring policy like p=none) and gradually move to enforcement.

findings.title: Server only negotiates TLS 1.2, not newer TLS 1.3
findings.explanation: The site's TLS certificate itself is valid for 60 more days, but the connection only used TLS 1.2. TLS 1.3 offers stronger security and better performance, and many modern browsers/servers support it by default.
findings.recommendation: Check server/TLS library configuration and enable TLS 1.3 support if the hosting stack allows it.

findings.title: Slow initial server response with no CDN in front of the site
findings.explanation: The site took 320ms to start sending data (time to first byte), which is on the slower side, and there's no CDN detected to help cache and speed up delivery for visitors, especially those farther from the server.
findings.recommendation: Consider enabling a CDN (e.g. Cloudflare) and/or server-side caching to reduce response times.
